pos: n. (a boundary; the utmost extent or point beyond which a thing does not or may not pass)
etymology: Latin limes, a boundary, a frontier, especially the fortified border of a Roman province. A limit is, at root, a marked edge, the line beyond which one territory ends and another begins.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel's closing vision of the restored temple ends its detailed measurements with a single, sweeping statement of the whole complex's outer boundary: Upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy. After chapter upon chapter of exact cubits for gates, chambers, and courts, the vision steps back to name the one fact that governs every measurement already given — the entire enclosed limit, not merely the innermost sanctuary, is most holy ground, a single boundary drawn around the whole rather than a series of graduated zones of lesser and greater sanctity.

The verse's placement matters as much as its content. It comes immediately after the command that the house's whole form, fashion, goings out, comings in, and laws be written down and kept, so that a people ashamed of their former sins might return to a pattern they can actually see and follow. A limit given in such exact, recorded detail is not an arbitrary restriction; it is the visible edge of a holiness the LORD Himself is willing to specify to the last cubit, precisely so that no one inside it could plausibly claim ignorance of where the boundary lay. Scripture's holiness is not vague to Ezekiel's audience; it has a limit, and the limit is drawn and measured before a single stone is set in place.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the utmost extent; the bound or boundary of a thing; the line or point beyond which a thing cannot or may not pass.
webster_full: LIMIT, n. The bound or utmost extent of a thing; a boundary line, real or imaginary, beyond which extension does not take place.
HOLY, a. Set apart for sacred use; free from sin; consecrated to the service of God.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most holy part of a temple; a place of protection.
MEASURE, v.t. To ascertain the dimensions, quantity, or extent of, by a fixed standard.
PATTERN, n. A model or original to be copied or imitated; a form or plan to be followed exactly.
scriptures: And if they be ashamed of all that they have done, shew them the form of the house, and the fashion thereof, and the goings out thereof, and the comings in thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the laws thereof: and write it in their sight, that they may keep the whole form thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and do them.
This is the law of the house; Upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the house.
He measured it by the four sides: it had a wall round about, five hundred reeds long, and five hundred broad, to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place.
And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;
corruption_summary: A limit is treated as an arbitrary restriction imposed to constrain freedom, when Ezekiel's temple limit is given in exact, recorded measurement precisely so that holiness would be knowable and followable rather than left to guesswork.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a limit still names a boundary. The principle worth recovering is why Ezekiel's vision bothers to measure the limit at all, down to the cubit, rather than simply declaring the temple holy in general terms. A limit that cannot be located is not a real limit; it is a vague warning that leaves everyone unsure how close they may safely come.

The command to write the whole pattern down, so that a people ashamed of their past sins could keep it, shows the limit functioning as mercy rather than mere restriction. Leviticus states the underlying principle plainly: putting a difference between holy and unholy is itself a duty, and a limit precisely drawn is how that difference becomes something ordinary people can actually recognize and honor, rather than a holiness so undefined it can only ever be transgressed by accident.
roots_summary: Hebrew gebul (H1366), a border, a boundary, a limit; the standing Old Testament word for territorial and sacred boundaries alike.
roots_lines: Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, boundary, limit; the noun rendered “limit” in Ezekiel 43:12, elsewhere used of tribal and national borders.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing, a sacred place; the quality declared of the whole limit, most holy.
Hebrew tokniyth (H8508) — a measurement, a proportion, a pattern; the standing word for the exact form Ezekiel is shown throughout the temple vision.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate, to make a distinction; the verb behind Leviticus 10:10's command to put a difference between holy and unholy.
Hebrew bosh (H954, in the sense of shame) — to be ashamed; the condition of the people the whole vision's exact pattern is meant to address, Ezekiel 43:10-11.
usage: “the whole limit thereof round about shall be most holy” — the boundary of Ezekiel's temple vision.
“write it in their sight, that they may keep the whole form thereof” — the exact pattern given so the limit could be known.
“put difference between holy and unholy” — the underlying principle a measured limit serves.

pos: n. (that which is lent; something given to another for temporary use, to be returned or repaid)
etymology: Old Norse lan, related to Saxon laenan, to lend, the same root as lend itself. A loan is, at root, simply the thing lent, understood on both sides as due to return.
biblical_def:
Scripture's two uses of the word describe loans of an entirely different order from one another, and the contrast is instructive. Deuteronomy's law of the pledge protects the dignity of a poor borrower even in the ordinary business of a loan: a lender may not enter a debtor's house to fetch the pledge himself, but must stand outside and let the borrower bring it out to him — an ordinary financial loan, hedged about with a mercy that keeps the transaction from becoming an occasion for humiliation.

First Samuel's use of the word describes a loan of a different kind entirely. Hannah, having vowed her long-awaited son to the LORD's service before he was even conceived, brings the child Samuel to Eli once he is weaned, and Eli's blessing on Elkanah and his wife recalls the transaction in exactly these terms: the LORD give thee seed of this woman for the loan which is lent to the LORD. Samuel himself is the loan — not owned outright by his mother even as her own son, but lent, on purpose, to the LORD's service for the whole of his life, in fulfillment of a vow made before he existed. Between an ordinary pledge treated with dignity and a son understood from before his birth as a loan lent to God, Scripture's two uses of the word span the whole range of what it means to hold something, however dearly loved, as never finally one's own to keep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which is lent; a sum of money or a thing given to another for temporary use, on condition of return or repayment.
webster_full: LOAN, n. That which is lent; a thing given to another with the understanding that it, or its equivalent, will be returned.
PLEDGE, n. Something deposited as security for the performance of a contract or repayment of a debt.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, binding the maker to a particular act, gift, or manner of life.
LEND, v.t. To grant the temporary use of, on condition that the thing lent, or its equivalent, be returned.
WEAN, v.t. To accustom a child to cease taking milk from the mother; to withdraw gradually from a former object of dependence.
scriptures: When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge.
Thou shalt stand abroad, and the man to whom thou dost lend shall bring out the pledge abroad unto thee.
Moreover his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year, when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, and said, The LORD give thee seed of this woman for the loan which is lent to the LORD. And they went unto their own home.
corruption_summary: A loan is treated as a purely commercial arrangement, morally neutral apart from its terms, when Hannah's own vow of Samuel shows Scripture using the same word for a child understood, from before conception, as never ultimately belonging to his mother at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain financial word; a loan still names what is lent with an expectation of return. The principle worth recovering runs through the deliberate dignity Deuteronomy's pledge-law builds into even the most ordinary of loans, refusing to let a lender's legitimate claim become an occasion to violate a poor debtor's home and privacy.

Hannah's loan is the more radical of the two, and the harder principle to hold. She does not merely dedicate Samuel in a general sense; Eli's blessing names him specifically as the loan which is lent to the LORD, language that treats a beloved, long-prayed-for son as never having been Hannah's final possession in the first place, only entrusted to her for a season before being returned, by her own glad vow, to the one who gave him. What Deuteronomy protects with dignity in an ordinary loan, Hannah offers up entirely in an extraordinary one.
roots_summary: Hebrew abat (H5670), to lend on pledge; Hebrew sha'al (H7592), to ask, to request, the very root of Samuel's own name and the verb behind “the loan which is lent” in 1 Samuel 2:20.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, to request, to lend; the root behind both Samuel's name (asked of the LORD) and the noun rendered “loan” in 1 Samuel 2:20.
Hebrew abat (H5670) — to lend on pledge, to borrow; the verb behind Deuteronomy 24:10's ordinary financial loan.
Hebrew abot (H5667) — a pledge, a thing given in security; the object Deuteronomy protects from the lender's own intrusion.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow; the solemn promise behind Hannah's dedication of Samuel before his birth.
Hebrew gamal (H1580, in the sense of weaning) — to wean, to deal fully with; the verb behind Samuel being brought to Eli once weaned, 1 Samuel 1:22-24.
usage: “the LORD give thee seed of this woman for the loan which is lent to the LORD” — Eli's blessing over Hannah and Elkanah.
“thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge” — the dignity Deuteronomy protects in an ordinary loan.
“his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year” — the ongoing love within the loan Hannah had made.

pos: n., v.t. (release from an obligation, burden, or post; to dismiss, acquit, or set free)
etymology: Old French descharger, from des-, undoing, and charger, to load or charge. A discharge is, at root, the unloading of a burden that had been placed on a person — a debt, a duty, a post, or, in the Preacher's stark use of the word, a war.
biblical_def:
Ecclesiastes' one use of the word belongs to one of the Preacher's bluntest observations on the limits of human power. Having noted that no man has power over the spirit to retain it, nor power in the day of death, he adds a third, deliberately chosen comparison: there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it. A soldier in an ordinary war might hope for a discharge, a formal release from further service; death, the Preacher insists, is a war with no such provision, no furlough, no honorable release before the appointed end.

The verse's second half closes off the one remaining hope a reader might still reach for: that wickedness, or at least the power and cunning that often accompany it, might buy some exemption where ordinary soldiering could not. The Preacher denies this specifically — wickedness delivers no one who is given to it, not from this particular war. Between the two halves of the verse, Ecclesiastes removes both the natural hope of an honorable discharge and the cynical hope of an unrighteous escape, leaving death as the one appointment from which Scripture, at least in this verse, offers no discharge of any kind to any man on his own terms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): release from an obligation, debt, or duty; dismissal from an office, employment, or post; acquittal.
webster_full: DISCHARGE, n. Release from an obligation, debt, penalty, or duty; dismissal from service or office.
RETAIN, v.t. To keep; to hold; to continue to possess, without loss or separation.
APPOINTED, a. Fixed, set, or ordained beforehand; determined by authority or decree.
WICKEDNESS, n. The quality of being wicked; departure from the rules of morality or religion; sin.
DELIVER, v.t. To rescue; to set free; to release from danger, confinement, or evil.
scriptures: Ecc 8:8

There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it.
Ecc 3:2
A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death? shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Selah.
corruption_summary: Death is treated as negotiable, delayable indefinitely by wealth, cunning, or power, when the Preacher's own comparison to a war with no discharge and the Hebrews' doctrine of an appointed day both deny any such exemption to any man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a discharge still names a release from service. The principle worth recovering is the Preacher's deliberate closing off of both routes a man might imagine toward escaping this particular war — not the honorable discharge an ordinary soldier might earn, and not the cynical exemption a wicked man might purchase through his very wickedness.

Hebrews' plain statement, that it is appointed unto men once to die, states as settled doctrine what Ecclesiastes reaches by hard observation, and Psalm 89 asks the same question as a rhetorical certainty, what man is he that liveth, and shall not see death. None of these texts counsel despair; together they simply remove the illusion of a discharge available on human terms, so that the only real hope left standing is not an escape from the appointment but a right standing for the judgment appointed to follow it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishlachath (H4917), a discharge, a sending away, from the root shalach (H7971), to send; the noun of Ecclesiastes 8:8's stark military comparison.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishlachath (H4917) — a discharge, a release, a sending forth; the rare noun rendered “discharge” in Ecclesiastes 8:8.
Hebrew shalach (H7971) — to send, to let go, to release; the common verb root behind mishlachath.
Hebrew milchamah (H4421) — war, battle; the figure the Preacher chooses for death's own inescapable summons.
Hebrew resha (H7562) — wickedness; explicitly denied any power to deliver its own from this particular war.
Greek apokeimai (G606) — to be laid up, to be reserved, appointed; the verb behind Hebrews 9:27's it is appointed unto men once to die.
usage: “there is no discharge in that war” — the Preacher's stark comparison of death to an inescapable war.
“neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it” — the second hope the same verse removes.
“it is appointed unto men once to die” — the doctrine that closes both hopes for good.

pos: v.t. (to uncover; to make known that which was hidden; to reveal)
etymology: Old French desclos, from Latin dis-, apart, and claudere, to close or shut. To disclose is, at root, the reverse of closing — the opening of what had been shut so that its contents can no longer stay concealed.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's apocalyptic close, promising a coming day of the LORD's judgment on the whole earth's iniquity, names one specific, disturbing sign of that day's arrival: the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain. The image reaches back to Genesis, to Cain's murdered brother whose blood cried out from the ground, and to Job's own protest, O earth, cover not thou my blood — a longstanding Old Testament expectation that innocent blood, once shed and buried, does not simply vanish into silence but is, in some sense, held by the ground it soaked into, awaiting a reckoning.

What Isaiah promises is the ground's own testimony finally given voice. Every quiet murder, every buried victim of violence the world called settled and forgotten, is pictured as evidence the earth herself has been keeping, unwilling forever to be the accomplice of concealment. The prophecy sits directly beside the command to Israel to hide herself briefly, as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast — God's own people sheltered from the storm of judgment even while the earth is commanded to stop covering what it once concealed. Disclosure, in this text, is not merely information revealed; it is the final undoing of every attempt, however successful for a time, to bury a wrong and call it finished.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to uncover; to lay open to view; to make known something secret or hidden; to reveal.
webster_full: DISCLOSE, v.t. To uncover; to lay open what was concealed; to reveal, as a secret or hidden fact.
CONCEAL, v.t. To hide; to withdraw from observation; to keep secret.
SLAIN, a. Killed, especially by violence; put to death in battle or by murder.
INIQUITY, n. Injustice; wickedness; a violation of right; a sin against moral law.
INDIGNATION, n. Strong displeasure at something considered unjust, mean, or wicked; here, of God's righteous anger.
scriptures: Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.
For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity: the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain.
Gen 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my cry have no place.
corruption_summary: Buried violence is treated as settled and finished once it disappears from public memory, when Isaiah's promise pictures the earth itself as an unwilling accomplice that will one day disclose, not keep, every drop of innocent blood it has ever covered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to disclose still means to uncover what was hidden. The principle worth recovering is how far back the expectation reaches. Abel's blood cries from the ground in the very first murder recorded in Scripture, and Job, centuries later, pleads with the earth itself not to cover his own innocent blood — both texts treating the ground not as a passive burial site but as a place that can, in some real sense, keep or surrender testimony.

Isaiah's prophecy promises the day that testimony will finally be surrendered in full, every concealed victim disclosed at last, and pairs that promise directly with a command to God's own people to hide themselves briefly while the reckoning falls. The lesson is not that concealment fails immediately or dramatically in this life — often it appears to succeed for a very long time — but that Scripture refuses to let a buried wrong count, in the end, as a wrong actually settled.
roots_summary: Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover, to reveal, to go into exile; the verb behind “disclose” in Isaiah 26:21, elsewhere used of prophetic revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to disclose, to reveal; the verb rendered “disclose” in Isaiah 26:21, also the root behind the Hebrew word for exile.
Hebrew kacah (H3680, negated) — to cover, to conceal; explicitly denied of the earth's slain in the same verse.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; the substance both Abel's and Job's texts describe the ground as keeping rather than absorbing silently.
Hebrew tsa'aq (H6817) — to cry out, to call for help; the verb of Abel's blood crying from the ground in Genesis 4:10.
Hebrew za'am (H2195) — indignation, wrathful denunciation; the coming judgment Israel is told to hide briefly from in Isaiah 26:20.
usage: “the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain” — Isaiah's promise of a final reckoning.
“the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” — the same principle at the first murder.
“O earth, cover not thou my blood” — Job's own plea against premature concealment.

pos: v.t., n. (to bring shame or dishonor upon; the state of being out of favor; shame; dishonor)
etymology: Old French desgracier, from dis-, undoing, and Latin gratia, favor or grace. To disgrace is, at root, to remove someone or something from a state of grace or favor — the exact opposite motion the word grace itself names.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah's one use of the word belongs to a prayer of national lament, offered on behalf of a people under judgment who nonetheless dare to plead the LORD's own honor as their ground of appeal: Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory: remember, break not thy covenant with us. The petition is careful and theologically precise. It does not primarily ask for Israel's own comfort; it argues that Israel's continued desolation would itself disgrace the throne of the LORD's own glory, since His name and His covenant people had, by His own choosing, become bound together in the world's sight.

The logic depends entirely on covenant, not on any remaining merit in the people making the plea — the same chapter freely confesses that their iniquities testify against them and their backslidings are many. What the prayer appeals to instead is the LORD's own reputation, staked publicly on His covenant with this particular people; to disgrace them beyond recovery would be, in the terms the prayer itself supplies, to disgrace the throne from which He reigns. It is a bold form of intercession, arguing not from the petitioner's worthiness but from the petitioned One's own glory, and it stands as one model for prayer offered by a people who have no claim left except the name they were called by.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to bring shame or reproach upon; to dishonor; also, the state of being out of favor, or in a condition of shame.
webster_full: DISGRACE, v.t. To bring reproach or shame upon; to dishonor; to treat with contempt or indignity.
ABHOR, v.t. To hate extremely; to detest; to regard with disgust and repugnance.
GLORY, n. Splendor; magnificence; honor and praise, especially as ascribed to God.
COVENANT, n. A solemn, binding agreement between parties, especially between God and his people.
INTERCESSION, n. The act of interceding; prayer or entreaty in favor of another, or on behalf of oneself before God.
scriptures: Jer 14:7
O LORD, though our iniquities testify against us, do thou it for thy name's sake: for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against thee.
Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory: remember, break not thy covenant with us.

Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; I do not this for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name's sake, which ye have profaned among the heathen, whither ye went.
Psa 79:9
Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake.
corruption_summary: Prayer is treated as valid only when it appeals to the petitioner's own worthiness or need, when Jeremiah's boldest intercession appeals instead to the LORD's own glory and covenant name, staking nothing on Israel's merit at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; disgrace still names shame or dishonor. The principle worth recovering is the specific shape of covenant intercession Jeremiah models here. He does not minimize Israel's guilt, confessing in the very same prayer that their iniquities testify against them and their backslidings are many; and he does not, on that basis, abandon hope, because the prayer's real argument was never Israel's worthiness in the first place.

Ezekiel's later oracle states the same principle even more starkly from the LORD's own side: I do not this for your sakes... but for mine holy name's sake. A people bound to God by covenant can appeal to His own glory precisely because His name has been publicly attached to their fate; to let them be disgraced beyond recovery would, by the very terms of the covenant He established, touch the honor of the throne itself. This is not presumption but the specific, textured logic of a prayer that has nothing left to offer except the name it was called by.
roots_summary: Hebrew na'ats (H5006), to despise, to spurn; the verb behind “disgrace” in Jeremiah 14:21, elsewhere rendered abhor or blaspheme.
roots_lines: Hebrew na'ats (H5006) — to despise, spurn, disgrace; the verb rendered “disgrace” in Jeremiah 14:21, elsewhere translated abhor or provoke.
Hebrew kavod (H3519) — glory, honor, weight; the noun behind “the throne of thy glory,” the LORD's own honor bound up with His people's fate.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the binding agreement the prayer appeals to and asks not to be broken.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to defile; the verb behind Ezekiel 36:22's account of the LORD's name profaned among the nations.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — name; the covenant name at stake in every one of these prayers, the ground of the appeal rather than the petitioners' own merit.
usage: “do not disgrace the throne of thy glory” — Jeremiah's bold covenant appeal.
“though our iniquities testify against us... do thou it for thy name's sake” — the confession the appeal is built on.
“I do not this for your sakes... but for mine holy name's sake” — the LORD's own statement of the same principle.

pos: v.t. (to merit, by services or conduct; to be worthy of reward or punishment)
etymology: Latin deservire, to serve zealously, from de-, thoroughly, and servire, to serve. To deserve is, at root, to have served thoroughly enough to have earned a due return, whether of reward or of penalty.
biblical_def:
Ezra's great confessional prayer, offered on behalf of the returned exiles after discovering their intermarriage with the surrounding nations, contains the Authorized Version's single use of this word, set inside a remarkable admission of undeserved mercy: after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this. Ezra does not plead that the exile and its sufferings were disproportionate; he states, as the premise of his whole prayer, that even the worst that had already fallen on Israel was less than what her iniquities genuinely deserved.

The confession is the opposite of the self-justifying instinct that measures suffering against merit and finds the accounting unfair. Ezra's arithmetic runs the other direction: whatever calamity Israel has actually endured is a mercy, calculated against a true deserving that would have warranted far worse, and the return from exile itself, the deliverance he is praying about, is likewise undeserved on any accounting of Israel's own conduct. A word most often used to demand what is owed to oneself is here used to confess how much worse than what one has already received would actually have been owed, and the whole prayer that follows is built on that reversal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to merit or be worthy of, by service, conduct, or qualities, either good or bad; to earn by desert.
webster_full: DESERVE, v.t. To merit; to be worthy of, whether reward or punishment, by one's actions or character.
TRESPASS, n. An offense; a transgression of duty, law, or the rights of another.
INIQUITY, n. Injustice; wickedness; gross violation of right or duty.
DELIVERANCE, n. The act of delivering or freeing; rescue from bondage, danger, or evil.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment of a fact, especially of guilt or sin; a public or private admission of wrongdoing.
scriptures: Ezr 9:6
And said, O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens.
Ezr 9:13

And after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this;
Ezr 9:15
O LORD God of Israel, thou art righteous: for we remain yet escaped, as it is this day: behold, we are before thee in our trespasses: for we cannot stand before thee because of this.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
corruption_summary: Deserving is invoked mainly to argue that one's suffering is unfair or excessive, when Ezra's own prayer uses the word to confess the opposite - that even severe judgment fell short of what was actually deserved.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; deserve still names what is merited by conduct. The principle worth recovering is the direction Ezra's confession runs. A natural instinct, faced with exile and loss, is to calculate whether the punishment fit the crime and to argue, if possible, that it did not; Ezra instead does the opposite math, insisting that the LORD hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve.

Lamentations supplies the doctrine that makes such a confession bearable rather than merely despairing: it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. Ezra's prayer and Jeremiah's lament together model a use of the word deserve almost opposite to its ordinary employment — not a demand for what is owed to the speaker, but an honest acknowledgment of how much worse than what has already been received would, by the speaker's own admission, have been entirely just.
roots_summary: Hebrew chasak (H2820), to withhold, to spare; the verb underlying the idiom “punished us less than,” literally withheld beneath our iniquities, in Ezra 9:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to withhold, to spare, to keep back; the verb behind the Hebrew idiom rendered “punished us less than our iniquities deserve,” literally withheld beneath.
Hebrew avon (H5771) — iniquity, guilt, punishment for iniquity; the noun measuring what was actually deserved.
Hebrew ma'al (H4604) — a trespass, an unfaithful act; the specific offense, intermarriage with the nations, confessed in Ezra 9.
Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous, just; the title Ezra gives the LORD in 9:15 even while confessing Israel's own guilt.
Hebrew checed (H2617) — steadfast covenant love, mercy; the quality Lamentations 3:22 credits for Israel's survival at all.
usage: “thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve” — Ezra's confession of undeserved mercy.
“we are before thee in our trespasses: for we cannot stand before thee” — the honest ground of the whole prayer.
“It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed” — the same principle from Lamentations.

pos: n. (guidance; the act of directing; the course or line along which a thing moves or is aimed)
etymology: Latin directio, from dirigere, to direct, from di- (dis-), apart, and regere, to rule or guide. Direction is, at root, the act of a ruling hand setting the straight course a thing is to follow.
biblical_def:
Numbers' brief travel notice, tucked between the itinerary of Israel's wilderness journey, records an act of communal labor accomplished under a specific, named authority: The princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it, by the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves. It is a small, almost incidental verse, celebrated immediately afterward in the Song of the Well, and yet its structure is worth noticing — the princes and nobles of Israel, men of real standing, do not dig according to their own preference or convenience, but by the direction of the lawgiver, using nothing more than their own staves as tools.

The picture is one of ordinary, cooperative labor placed under a single, recognized direction, and celebrated in song precisely because it succeeded. No miracle produces the well; leaders of the people, working by hand with common staves, dig it themselves, and the difference between this labor and mere digging is the direction it was undertaken under — Moses' own authority, itself received from the LORD who had promised the water in the first place. A well dug by direction, however ordinary the tools, becomes an occasion for a whole nation's song; the same labor undertaken without any recognized direction would have remained merely a well.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of directing; guidance; instruction as to a course to be followed; the line or point toward which anything moves or is aimed.
webster_full: DIRECTION, n. The act of directing; guidance; also, the course or line pointed out for movement or action.
LAWGIVER, n. One who makes or enacts laws; especially, a leader authorized to establish rules for a people.
STAVES, n. pl. of staff; a stick or rod used as a support, weapon, or tool.
PRINCE, n. A person of high rank; a chief; a ruler or leader among a people.
AUTHORITY, n. Legitimate power to command, act, or decide; the right to direct the actions of others.
scriptures: And from thence they went to Beer: that is the well whereof the LORD spake unto Moses, Gather the people together, and I will give them water.
Then Israel sang this song, Spring up, O well; sing ye unto it:
The princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it, by the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves. And from the wilderness they went to Mattanah:
Pro 3:6
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
corruption_summary: Direction from recognized authority is treated as an obstacle to genuine cooperation, when the well of Beer is dug by willing, capable leaders precisely under a single, acknowledged direction, and celebrated in song for exactly that reason.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; direction still names guidance toward a course. The principle worth recovering is how little the text credits the well's success to the raw ability of the princes and nobles who did the actual digging, real as that ability was, and how much weight it places instead on the single word by the direction of the lawgiver.

Proverbs states as a general principle what Numbers shows in one specific, sung episode: in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. The leaders at Beer had staves and standing enough to dig a well on their own initiative if they had chosen to; the song that follows celebrates not merely water found, but labor rightly directed, ordinary strength placed under a recognized authority and, for that reason, made the subject of Israel's own praise.
roots_summary: Hebrew choqeq (H2710), a lawgiver, one who decrees; the title behind “the direction of the lawgiver” in Numbers 21:18, from the verb to engrave or decree.
roots_lines: Hebrew choqeq (H2710) — a lawgiver, a decree-maker; the title rendered “the lawgiver” in Numbers 21:18, from a root meaning to engrave or inscribe a decree.
Hebrew chaphar (H2658) — to dig, to search out; the verb of the princes' and nobles' own labor at the well.
Hebrew nadiyb (H5081) — a noble, a willing, generous man; the title of the second group of diggers, alongside the princes.
Hebrew mishe'enah (H4938, related to staff) — a staff, a support; the plain tool named alongside their digging.
Hebrew yashar (H3474, root behind “direct”) — to be straight, to go directly; the underlying idea in Proverbs 3:6's promise that the LORD shall direct thy paths.
usage: “The princes digged the well... by the direction of the lawgiver” — ordinary labor placed under recognized authority.
“Then Israel sang this song, Spring up, O well” — the celebration that followed.
“In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths” — the general principle behind the specific episode.

pos: v.t., v.i. (to set oneself against; to resist; to act in opposition to)
etymology: Latin opponere, from ob-, against, and ponere, to place or set. To oppose is, at root, to set oneself directly against another, placed in the opposing position.
biblical_def:
Paul's instruction to Timothy on how a servant of the Lord ought to conduct himself toward opponents uses the word in a construction easy to misread on a fast pass: In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. The men in view are not merely Timothy's opponents in some external sense; they oppose themselves, working, in their resistance to the truth, against their own actual good, entangled in a snare they did not fully choose and cannot simply reason their own way out of.

The instruction that surrounds this diagnosis is deliberately unlike the response such opposition usually provokes. The servant of the Lord must not strive, Paul says, but be gentle to all men, apt to teach, patient, instructing his opponents in meekness rather than matching their opposition with equal force — not because the opposition is unserious, but because Paul names its cause as a snare of the devil, the very kind of captivity that force cannot free a man from. The hoped-for outcome is not victory in an argument but that God, peradventure, will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth, an outcome only God can grant, and one Paul's whole instruction is calibrated to leave room for rather than to force by superior argument or superior pressure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to act against; to place in opposition; to resist by argument, contrary conduct, or force.
webster_full: OPPOSE, v.t. To act against; to place in the way of; to resist, whether by argument, contrary measures, or open hostility.
MEEKNESS, n. Gentleness of temper; mildness; softness of disposition; patience under injury.
SNARE, n. A trap; something that entangles or entraps an unwary person, whether physically or morally.
REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow for sin, with a genuine turning away from it; a change of mind and heart toward God.
STRIVE, v.i. To contend; to struggle in opposition; to quarrel or dispute earnestly.
scriptures: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: Opposition to the truth is treated as an intellectual failure to be defeated by superior argument, when Paul diagnoses it as a snare of the devil, a captivity requiring meekness and prayer for repentance rather than the greater force of a stronger opponent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to oppose still means to set oneself against. The principle worth recovering is Paul's specific diagnosis of what is happening inside a person who opposes the truth — not merely a mistaken opinion awaiting correction by a better argument, but a man taken captive by the devil at his will, opposing his own actual good even as he opposes Timothy.

The prescribed response follows directly from that diagnosis. A servant of the Lord must not strive, matching opposition with equal force, but instruct in meekness, because the goal is not to win an argument against an opponent but to see a captive recover himself out of a snare he did not fully choose. Galatians' parallel instruction, to restore a fallen brother in the spirit of meekness while considering oneself, lest thou also be tempted, shows the same posture extended even to a brother's fault rather than an outsider's opposition.
roots_summary: Greek antidiatithemi (G475), to oppose oneself, to be set in opposition; the rare middle-voice verb behind “oppose themselves” in 2 Timothy 2:25, used only here in the New Testament.
roots_lines: Greek antidiatithemi (G475) — to set oneself in opposition, to oppose oneself; a rare compound verb, used only at 2 Timothy 2:25.
Greek praotes (G4236) — meekness, gentleness; the manner Paul prescribes for instructing such opponents.
Greek pagis (G3803) — a snare, a trap; the word naming the devil's own device that has captured the opponent.
Greek zogreo (G2221) — to catch alive, to take captive; the verb behind “taken captive by him at his will” in 2 Timothy 2:26.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance, a change of mind; the outcome Paul hopes God will grant even to a hardened opponent.
usage: “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” — Paul's instruction on confronting opposition to the truth.
“taken captive by him at his will” — the diagnosis behind that opposition.
“restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” — the same posture applied to a brother's fault.

pos: a. (lowest; situated at the bottom; the superlative of nether)
etymology: Saxon nither, down, below, with the superlative ending -most — the very lowest, the bottommost of a graduated series, as opposed to something merely low among two.
biblical_def:
Solomon's temple, as First Kings describes its construction, was surrounded on three sides by a structure of side chambers built up against its outer wall in three ascending stories, and the text takes care to name the lowest of the three by its exact width: The nethermost chamber was five cubits broad, and the middle was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. Each story widens as it rises, an architectural detail made possible by rebatements cut into the temple wall itself so that the supporting beams of each higher chamber could rest without being fastened directly into the temple's own sacred stonework.

The nethermost chamber, narrowest and lowest of the three, was not therefore the least considered; the text specifies its exact measurement with the same careful attention given to the chambers above it, and the whole arrangement exists precisely so that no beam would need to violate the temple wall to support any story, including the bottom one. Scripture elsewhere uses the same word figuratively of the lowest imaginable extremity, the nethermost part of the pit or the depths of divine wrath kindled to the nethermost hell, and the temple's own careful measurement of its nethermost chamber offers a quiet counterpoint: even the lowest tier of a structure built for the LORD's own house is measured, named, and built with the same exactness as every story above it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): lowest; being in the lowest place or degree; the superlative of nether.
webster_full: NETHERMOST, a. Lowest; being at the bottom, or in the lowest place, of a graduated series.
CHAMBER, n. A room, especially a private or inner room; here, one of the side structures built against the temple wall.
CUBIT, n. An ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
REBATEMENT, n. A recess or ledge cut into a wall to receive and support a beam without piercing the wall itself.
TEMPLE, n. A building set apart for the worship of God; specifically, the house built by Solomon in Jerusalem.
scriptures: And against the wall of the house he built chambers round about, against the walls of the house round about, both of the temple and of the oracle: and he made chambers round about:

The nethermost chamber was five cubits broad, and the middle was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad: for without in the wall of the house he made narrowed rests round about, that the beams should not be fastened in the walls of the house.
The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third.
For a fire is kindled in mine anger, and shall burn unto the lowest hell, and shall consume the earth with her increase, and set on fire the foundations of the mountains.
corruption_summary: The lowest tier of any structure is assumed to receive the least care or exactness, when the temple's nethermost chamber is measured, named, and built with the same precision given to the stories above it, none of them violating the sacred wall they surround.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; nethermost still names the lowest of a series. The principle worth recovering is the exactness the text spends on a chamber that, by definition, occupies the least prestigious position in the whole three-story structure. Its five-cubit width is recorded with the same specificity as the middle chamber's six and the third's seven, and the ingenious rebatement system exists precisely so that even this lowest, narrowest chamber could be built without a single beam piercing the temple's own consecrated wall.

Deuteronomy's figurative use of the same root, a fire burning unto the lowest hell, shows the word's range extending to the direst possible extremity of divine judgment. Read against that figurative depth, the temple's own carefully measured nethermost chamber stands as a small, practical witness to a larger principle: nothing built for the LORD's house, not even its lowest and least conspicuous story, was exempt from exact and deliberate craftsmanship.
roots_summary: Hebrew tachtown (H8481), lowest, nethermost; the superlative form behind “the nethermost chamber” in 1 Kings 6:6, from tachath, beneath.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachtown (H8481) — lowest, nethermost, undermost; the superlative adjective rendered “nethermost” in 1 Kings 6:6.
Hebrew tachath (H8478) — beneath, under, instead of; the root preposition behind tachtown.
Hebrew tsela (H6763) — a side, a rib, a chamber; the word for the side-chambers built against the temple wall.
Hebrew migra'ah (H4052, related) or a term for rebatement/ledge — the recess cut into the wall so beams need not pierce it.
Hebrew she'owl (H7585, paired with “lowest” in Deuteronomy 32:22) — the grave, the unseen realm of the dead, the figurative extremity of the same root idea.
usage: “The nethermost chamber was five cubits broad” — the exact measurement of the temple's lowest side-chamber.
“the beams should not be fastened in the walls of the house” — the careful design protecting even this lowest chamber's construction.
“shall burn unto the lowest hell” — the same root's figurative reach toward the direst extremity.

pos: v.t. (to expose to danger, loss, or destruction; to put at hazard)
etymology: Old French en-, to put into, and danger, from Latin dominus, a lord or master, through the sense of being under another's power. To endanger is, at root, to place someone under a power that could destroy them — originally, to put them at another's mercy.
biblical_def:
The prince of the eunuchs, hearing Daniel's request to be tested on pulse and water rather than the king's rich portion, answers with a fear that is entirely reasonable given his own position: I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king. The eunuch does not doubt Daniel's sincerity; he doubts his own safety, calculating with precision what would happen to him personally if Daniel's experiment failed and the king noticed his captives looking worse-fed than their peers.

What the rest of the chapter shows is a request carefully shaped to remove exactly this danger without asking the eunuch to risk anything on Daniel's behalf. Daniel does not ask him to disobey the king outright; he asks Melzar, a lesser steward, for a ten-day trial, small enough in scope that the greater official's own head was never actually put at risk by it, and the visible result, the four youths fairer and fatter than the rest, removes the danger from Melzar just as surely. Daniel's wisdom in this chapter is not merely spiritual; it is the practical skill of pursuing a costly obedience without needlessly endangering the men whose cooperation that obedience required, a kind of care for others even in the act of standing firm for himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to bring into danger or peril; to expose to loss, injury, or destruction; to hazard.
webster_full: ENDANGER, v.t. To expose to danger; to bring into peril or hazard, especially of loss or injury.
APPOINT, v.t. To fix, establish, or ordain, as by authority; to assign or allot.
EUNUCH, n. An officer of a royal or noble household, especially in the ancient Near East, often having charge of the harem or personal service.
PROVE, v.t. To test; to try by experiment or experience; to demonstrate the quality of something.
STEWARD, n. One appointed to manage the household affairs of another; an officer entrusted with provisions or supplies.
scriptures: Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Dan 1:9
Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs.
Dan 1:10

And the prince of the eunuchs said unto Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king.
Dan 1:12
Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.
corruption_summary: Faithful conviction is treated as licensing indifference to the real risks it creates for others, when Daniel's own request is shaped precisely to secure his obedience without needlessly endangering the officials whose cooperation he needed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to endanger still means to expose to hazard. The principle worth recovering is the practical wisdom Daniel shows in response to a fear the text does not treat as cowardice or unbelief. The prince of the eunuchs has a legitimate concern, that visible failure would cost him his own head, and Daniel's answer does not dismiss that concern as beneath his notice.

Instead Daniel proposes a bounded, low-risk test to a lesser official, Melzar, whose own head was never staked on the outcome the way the prince's would have been, and lets the visible ten-day result make the case rather than demanding blind trust from a man with everything to lose. A conviction firm enough to refuse the king's own meat did not, in Daniel's hands, require endangering anyone else's safety to be honored; the chapter's quiet lesson is that faithfulness and consideration for those put at risk by one's own stand are not, in fact, at odds.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayyab (H2325, in the sense of owing or being liable), root related to the idiom behind “endanger my head” in Daniel 1:10, a figure for personal, mortal liability before the king.
roots_lines: Hebrew idiom chayyab rosh — to make liable in respect of the head; the figure behind “endanger my head” in Daniel 1:10, mortal personal liability.
Hebrew yare' (H3372) — to fear, to be afraid; the verb of the eunuch's own stated concern.
Hebrew tsalach or Aramaic bachan (H974, cognate) — to test, to prove; the verb behind Daniel's own proposed trial in 1:12.
Hebrew chen (H2580) — favor, grace; the standing of Daniel before the prince of the eunuchs, granted by God in 1:9.
Hebrew mar'eh (H4758) — appearance, sight, countenance; the visible measure the whole test would be judged by.
usage: “then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king” — the eunuch's honest, reasonable fear.
“Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days” — Daniel's answer, shaped to remove that danger.
“God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love” — the providence that made such a careful request possible at all.
